question: A 45-year-old man is admitted with profuse watery diarrhoea for 3 days. He is cold peripherally, tachycardic (HR 118/min), hypotensive (BP 84/52 mmHg) and has flat neck veins. Central venous pressure is 1 cmH₂O. Which type of shock does this picture best represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cardiogenic shock shows raised filling pressures (raised JVP/CVP), not the flat neck veins and low CVP seen here.
Distributive shock typically presents with a hyperdynamic circulation (bounding pulse, warm peripheries) early on, not cold peripheries.
Correct. Loss of intravascular volume from diarrhoea produces hypovolaemic shock: cold peripheries, tachycardia, hypotension and low filling pressures (flat neck veins, CVP 1 cmH₂O).
Obstructive shock (e.g. tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade) typically shows raised venous pressures, not the low-pressure picture seen here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four classes of shock and the key differentiating haemodynamic features of each.
Well done. Hypovolaemia from fluid loss reduces preload, producing the classic low-pressure picture.
